topic: Nopus: Deterministic Prose Checks for Clearer Coding-Agent Responses
summary: nopus (npm @syzom/nopus, MIT, by GitHub user Vistyy) is a small deterministic prose checker that sits on a coding agent's Stop hook: when an assistant finishes a response, it measures the prose with packaged lexical data — word rarity, word concreteness, noun/modifier stacks, phrase density and a short allowlist of formulaic cues — and only if several measurements cross their thresholds together does it send the same agent a single instruction to rewrite the response more clearly. The pitch is the inverse of an LLM critic: the decision is reproducible, the checks are offline, no second model judges your prose, and there is at most one automatic rewrite so no retry loop is possible. It supports Pi, Claude Code and Codex. On the evidence, it is a well-scoped, unusually well-documented one-trick extension whose public numbers (9.9% rewrite rate at default sensitivity on a 5,337-response private Pi corpus, 41/50 human-label agreement on a medium-anchor batch) are self-reported and not independently reproducible, and whose repository has been quiet since 2026-08-19. Worth installing for people who are annoyed by lecture-hall framing and abstract 'capability/governance' prose from their agent; not a general-purpose AI-slop detector, not a substitute for a style guide, and not yet something to adopt site-wide without pinning the version.

nopus catches coding-agent answers that 'disappear into abstract LLM babble'; deterministic prose checks flag responses over a chosen complexity threshold and send them back for one clearer rewrite.
Supports three hosts only: Pi (npm:@syzom/nopus), Claude Code (plugin marketplace add Vistyy/nopus; nopus@nopus), Codex (codex plugin marketplace add). Node.js 22+ required.

Both Claude Code and Codex integrations work through a bounded Stop hook that requests exactly one clearer response; Pi uses an extension that can hide the rejected response from the terminal transcript.
Seven measurements: uncommon wording, very uncommon wording, abstract vocabulary, abstract sentences, noun/modifier stacks (3+ words), phrase load per 100 words, formulaic style cues.

Anti-over-trigger design: strips code blocks, inline code, URLs, file paths and table rows before measuring; proportions and phrase density instead of raw length; most decision paths need several measurements to cross together; at most one automatic rewrite so it cannot loop.
Sensitivity low/medium/high with published observed rewrite rates 5.3% / 9.9% / 18.6%, measured on 5,337 completed Pi responses from 515 session files.

Data provenance is checksum-pinned: claudisms.ai style cues (SHA-256 f4a09fa8...), SUBTLEX-US conversational frequencies (ISC), Norvig/Google Web Trillion word counts, Brysbaert concreteness ratings, Carpentries Glosario (CC-BY-4.0).
2026-08-14 private corpus: 5,337 unique completed Pi assistant responses from 515 session files; policy rewrites 284 (low, 5.3%), 531 (medium, 9.9%), 995 (high, 18.6%).

Human review is deliberately small: 50 labels on medium-sensitivity batches; policy agrees with 41, wrongly rewrites 5 accepted responses, misses 4. The author states the batches targeted the medium boundary and are NOT a representative population sample.
Verification distinguishes analyzer drift, policy drift on frozen measurements and end-to-end drift, and asserts decisions stay monotonic from low through high sensitivity.

Rewrite-model eval (2026-08-16, openai-codex/gpt-5.6-luna): 12 historical branches produced 4 medium-flagged originals; the normal rewrite passed the medium policy in 2 cases, the extra-simple rewrite in 3; extra-simple cut 279->45, 287->106 and 435->156 words. A public regression fixture exercises 5,000+ policy inputs but deliberately contains no response text, so the private corpus stays authoritative for drift detection.

CAUTION: its star chip reads 154 while the GitHub API returned 296 for the same repo; the page itself notes its metrics are 'heuristic approximations ... not authoritative measurements'. Do not cite its numbers.

REQUIRED CORRECTION SOURCE: this page fabricates specifics that do not exist in the project. It claims a reference paper 'Reducing Hallucinations in Coding Agents via Prose Constraints' (2026, arXiv:2607.89123) — arXiv returns 404 Article not found for that ID.

It also claims: 12+ prose/coding rules that block 'I think'/'maybe', code-block fencing validation, a browser runtime and CDN bundle, a CLI wrapper, 'npm install @vistyy/nopus', 98% coding-agent specificity and 67% hallucination-reduction rates, 3 community adapters including a Slack bot, and Claude Code 'sidebar integration'.

Everything above contradicts the authoritative README and src: there are 7 measurements and 6 rewrite signals, three host integrations, no browser target, no CDN, and no hallucination-rate claim anywhere in the repo.
Its own trend chip shows '4 stars' versus 296 actual. Use this page only as an example of the low-quality 'repo review' content now flooding search results for agent tooling.
Feature-list summary (configurable sensitivity, evidence output, extra-simple mode, technical-term exclusion) that matches the README.
Useful for its explicit advantage/limitation framing: consistent behavior from deterministic measurement, but measurement quality depends on packaged English word data.

stats.fact: npm package @syzom/nopus: only two published versions — 1.0.0 on 2026-08-15T13:11Z and 1.1.0 on 2026-08-16T13:45Z (latest). No runtime dependencies (zero-dependency install), engines node>=22.
Download volume is genuinely small: 204 npm downloads in the last month and 34 in the last week (window ending 2026-09-29).

Evaluation corpus: 5,337 unique completed Pi assistant responses from 515 session files (extracted 2026-08-14); the policy rewrites 284 / 531 / 995 responses at low / medium / high sensitivity = 5.3% / 9.9% / 18.6%.

Only human-labeled evidence published: 50 labels on medium-sensitivity batches, where the policy agreed with 41, incorrectly rewrote 5 accepted responses, and missed 4 responses marked for rewrite — and the authors state the second batch was deliberately sampled at the medium boundary, so it is not a representative population sample.

Rewrite-model evaluation (2026-08-16, openai-codex/gpt-5.6-luna, medium thinking): 12 historical branches tried, 4 originals selected by the medium policy; the normal rewrite passed the policy in 2 cases, the extra-simple rewrite in 3; extra-simple compressed 279→45, 287→106 and 435→156 words in the three substantial examples.

Seven measured signals: uncommon wording, very uncommon wording, abstract vocabulary, abstract sentences, noun and modifier stacks (3+ compressed), phrase load, and formulaic style cues — with word rarity from packaged conversational/broad-web frequency data and abstractness from human-rated concreteness norms plus a computing glossary.

Default configuration: complexitySensitivity=medium, includeEvidence=true, extraSimple=false, pi.hideOriginalResponse=true; overridable with NOPUS_COMPLEXITY_SENSITIVITY, NOPUS_INCLUDE_EVIDENCE, NOPUS_EXTRA_SIMPLE, NOPUS_PI_HIDE_ORIGINAL_RESPONSE, and the config lives at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nopus/config.json.

False-positive guards are explicit and testable: code blocks, inline code, URLs, file paths and table rows are stripped before measuring; obvious identifiers are excluded and established computing terms down-weighted; most decision paths need several measurements to cross thresholds together; a single rare word or dense phrase does not normally trigger; style cues need two distinct cues or one cue backed by uncommon wording; at most one automatic rewrite is requested (no loop).

Host support and mechanism: Pi (extension, lifecycle hooks, hides the rejected response by default), Claude Code (Stop hook via '/plugin marketplace add Vistyy/nopus' + '/plugin install nopus@nopus'), Codex ('codex plugin marketplace add Vistyy/nopus' + 'codex plugin add nopus@nopus'). Requires Node.js 22+.

Evaluation tooling is TypeScript/pnpm with devDependencies pinned to specific agent versions (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent 0.84.1, @anthropic-ai/claude-code 2.1.232, @openai/codex 0.147.0) and wink-nlp 2.4.0 + wink-eng-lite-web-model 1.8.1 for the language measurements.

The private corpus is deliberately not published (mode 0700, artefacts 0600, nothing committed); the repo ships only a public regression fixture of frozen scalar measurements exercising 'more than 5,000 policy inputs'. Peer reproduction of the headline rates is therefore impossible from the repo alone.

Context for adoption: Pi is a minimal MIT terminal coding agent by Mario Zechner (Earendil Inc.) with 4 built-in tools, a ~1k-token system prompt, and no sandboxing by default — extensions run in-process with the user's full permissions, so a prose-checking extension is also an arbitrary-code dependency. Pi's own docs say to review package source before installing.

Prior art is old and much larger: write-good (5,092 stars, 266,386 npm downloads last month, last publish 2022) and alex (184,122 downloads last month) lint English prose; Vale (6,175 stars) enforces house style; proselint (4,579 stars, 314 downloads last month) is effectively dormant. None of them run on an agent's response as a rewrite trigger.

The closest modern rival is avoid-ai-writing (4,803 stars; its avoid-ai-writing-detector npm package published 2026-08-02, last modified 2026-09-23, 2,092 downloads last month), which targets AI-writing tells in *content* and explicitly defers house style to Vale — a different job from nopus's 'this response was too hard to read, rewrite it'.

Related but distinct community projects show the category is active: Foremerge (521 stars, intent-conflict detection between parallel coding agents), anti-ai-slop (91 stars, a four-gate rewrite skill with a 37-pattern tell list including negative parallelism, throat-clearing openers, colon reveals and fake-profound endings).

Public discussion of nopus on Hacker News is absent: the HN Algolia API returns zero hits for the repository URL and no story for the project (searches for 'nopus', 'nopus coding agent' and 'deterministic prose checks' return unrelated Nginx/NOBUS/Nous results, nbHits 0 for the URL-restricted query).
GitHub repo Vistyy/nopus: 296 stars, 11 forks, 1 open issue, MIT license, TypeScript, created 2026-08-15, last push 2026-08-19.
Two releases only: v1.0.0 on 2026-08-15 and v1.1.0 on 2026-08-16; newest commit 2026-08-19 'Align pnpm toolchain configuration'. The project has been quiet for roughly six weeks.
The only open issue is #1 'Add OpenCode plugin support' (opened 2026-09-01, zero comments) — the top requested integration is still unbuilt.

Decision policy is six independent signal paths (sustained-abstractness, combined-complexity, stacked-phrasing, concentrated-complexity, pervasive-complexity, style-cues); a rewrite fires when ANY one is true.

stats.fact: Zero Hacker News presence: Algolia exact query for 'nopus' returns 0 stories. The launch ran through Reddit r/codex, LinkedIn, YouTube Shorts and Facebook/Instagram video instead.
No real research paper backs nopus. arXiv:2607.89123, which a third-party 'analysis' page cites as its reference implementation paper, returns 404 Article not found.

The academic case for verbosity filtering is real though: 'Verbosity Bias in Preference Labeling by Large Language Models' (arXiv:2310.10076, 2023-10-16) shows LLM judges prefer more verbose answers of similar quality.
'Verbosity != Veracity' (arXiv:2411.07858, 2024-11-12, v2 2024-12-07) documents verbosity compensation behaviour in LLMs.

'Verbosity-Aware Rationale Reduction' (arXiv:2412.21006, ACL 2025 Findings) removed redundant reasoning sentences for an average +7.71% task performance while cutting token generation 19.87% — i.e. trimming verbosity can improve accuracy, not just readability.

Developer pain is well measured: Stack Overflow's 2025 survey found 46% of developers distrust AI accuracy versus 33% who trust it (3% highly trust); 66% name 'almost right, but not quite' as their top frustration and 45% say debugging AI code takes longer.

Agent adoption roughly doubled while sentiment cooled: agents 31% (2025) to 59% (April 2026 pulse), Claude Code 41% to 55% in the same pulse, while trust in AI answers fell to 29% in 2025 (down 11 points).

Sonar's 2026 State of Code survey (1,100+ respondents): 96% do not fully trust AI-generated code is functionally correct, only 48% always check AI code before committing, 61% agree AI 'often produces code that looks correct but isn't reliable', and 40% cite unnecessary or duplicative code as a technical-debt harm.
stats.source: sonarsource.com State of Code Developer Survey report

stats.fact: AI slop is now a studied phenomenon: 'The Growing Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development' (arXiv:2603.27249) codes 1,154 Reddit/HN posts across 15 threads into Review Friction, Quality Degradation and Forces/Consequences clusters, and names verbose style as an explicit detection marker reviewers use.

Established prose-linter incumbents dwarf the agent-native entrants: vale 6,175 stars (actively maintained, pushed 2026-09-28), alex 5,102 stars (last push 2024-11-27), write-good 5,092 stars (2025-03-10).

A 2026 wave of small agent-skill prose linters exists but is tiny: openprose/prose-lint (Rust LSP/WASM, 4 stars), onlydole/tailord (3), erastudil/gfc (1), bkmashiro/prose-lint (0), YOOGOMJA/korean-prose-lint (0), beweiskette/schreibwaechter (German, 0).
stats.note: Korean and German variants signal the English-only gap is being filled from the edges.

stats.fact: HN discussion around AI-writing tells is warm but small: 'I'm sick of Claudisms, & what will happen next in AI-boosted software dev' 19 points (2026-09-23) and 'Claudisms - a living banlist of AI-writing tells' 4 points (2026-09-08); the broader 'AI slop' topic hits 834 points.

angles: Deterministic, not a second LLM: the accept/rewrite decision is a reproducible offline measurement, so the same prose and sensitivity always produce the same verdict — verify it by running the policy twice rather than trusting a judge model.

It fixes the response, not the session: the rejected answer is still in the model's history (and nopus only hides it from the Pi transcript), so the agent's reasoning about the task is unchanged — you are buying readability, not correctness.

The bounded-retry design is the interesting engineering choice: exactly one automatic rewrite means the tool cannot create an infinite politeness loop the way a critic-model hook can, at the cost of never fixing a response that is bad twice.

The evidence is self-reported and structurally unreproducible: 5,337 responses and 50 labels all come from a single author's private Pi corpus, and the corpus is intentionally not published — so any '9.9% rewrite rate' claim in a comparison table needs that caveat attached.

Fifty labels is a small sample: 41 agreements / 5 wrong rewrites / 4 misses is a useful directional signal (roughly four in five correct on a boundary-heavy batch) but the batch was sampled *at* the boundary, biasing it toward hard cases — the honest reading is that the numbers bound nothing in either direction.

The 'prose linter' lineage matters for positioning: write-good, alex, proselint and Vale already measure prose, but for humans writing documents in a CI gate; nopus is the first of that family wired as an agent response hook with a rewrite instruction as the output.

False positives on technical writing are the real adoption risk: the whole design defence is 'we strip code, paths, tables and identifiers' — which means the failure mode is legitimate dense abstraction in genuinely abstract discussions (authorization models, governance, capability boundaries) being told to rewrite.

Distribution is the agent-package catalog, not the developer-tool press: 296 stars, 204 npm downloads a month and zero Hacker News threads suggest a small but real niche audience of Pi/Claude Code users who found it via agentmods/pi.dev/claudepluginhub rather than a launch moment.

Maintenance signal is a real risk with a happy rider: no commits since 2026-08-19 and only two npm versions, but star growth continues (+7 to +10 a week in the agentmods snapshots) — an unmaintained extension that runs in-process with full user permissions is exactly the kind of dependency to pin and read.

Pi's trust model is the under-discussed part: extensions execute arbitrary code, project-local ones load only after a trust prompt, and nopus additionally *hides a response from the transcript* — a small, deliberate change to what the user sees, which is worth knowing before turning it on.

Determinism as the differentiator: no model, no ML, no prompt tuning — the same prose and sensitivity always produce the same verdict. Contrast with 'be concise' system prompts that burn context and enforce inconsistently.

The threshold table is the story: nopus publishes six signal paths and their literal numeric thresholds per sensitivity level, so a reviewer can audit exactly when an agent gets interrupted instead of trusting a black box.

Evidence quality is unusually honest for a tool this small: the author publishes the 5,337-response corpus size, the 5.3/9.9/18.6% rewrite rates, AND the uncomfortable human-label result (50 labels, 5 false rewrites, 4 misses, not a representative sample). Reward the honesty, and size the claim accordingly.

The English-only wall: SUBTLEX, Norvig counts and Brysbaert ratings are English datasets with no multilingual equivalents packaged. Code-switching or non-English responses produce meaningless metrics. This is the single biggest adoption blocker for non-English teams.

It cannot save tokens: nopus evaluates completed responses, so the 'babble' was already generated and billed. The only savings are human reading time and transcript clutter. Anyone expecting cost reduction is buying the wrong tool.

The hidden-response caveat: in Pi the rejected response is hidden from the terminal transcript but stays in the session and model history. Teams with transcript-based audit trails should know the visible record and the actual context diverge.

Six weeks of silence: two releases in two days in mid-August 2026, one commit on 2026-08-19, and the most requested integration (OpenCode, issue #1) still open with zero comments. Treat this as a promising single-maintainer experiment, not infrastructure.

Third-party 'reviews' of nopus are already hallucinating: an aggregator page invents an arXiv paper (404), a browser runtime, a CDN bundle, a CLI wrapper, 98%/67% effectiveness numbers and a Slack adapter that do not exist. Perfect case study for why agent-tooling research must go to the repo.

Verbosity filtering has real academic backing even though nopus itself has none: verbosity bias in LLM judging (2310.10076) and verbosity-aware rationale reduction improving accuracy +7.71% while cutting tokens 19.87% (2412.21006). The concept is sound; nopus is one small implementation of it.

Market timing: agent use doubled to 59% while trust fell to 29% and 96% of developers still do not fully trust AI code. Deterministic, auditable output guards are exactly the category this trust gap creates demand for — with Vale (6.2k stars) already owning the general prose-linting slot.

Host asymmetry: nopus ships as a plugin for the three most-used agent CLIs (Claude Code 14.5M weekly downloads, Codex 25.7M, Pi 4.3M) yet has 34 weekly downloads itself — a distribution gap worth explaining, not hiding.
